items.title: Was Madrid F1 race an economic upgrade on Barcelona?
items.author: Samarth Kanal
items.content:
The inaugural 2026 Spanish Formula 1 Grand Prix at the Madring created €544 million in economic activity, supported 10,948 jobs, and generated €95m in tax revenue, according to its organiser.

The Madring is a part-street circuit built around the IFEMA conference centre - with the track layout set to be changed for 2027 to improve the quality of racing and frequency of overtaking.

The grand prix promoter ran a study conducted by PwC showing that, for every €1 of economic activity directly linked to the event, €4.60 was generated across Madrid’s wider economy.

The total economic impact was 16.5% larger than expected, the grand prix supported 23.7% more jobs than anticipated, and the overall tax contribution was 14.5% more than predicted.

In comparison to Madrid’s figure of €544m in economic activity for 2026, the Barcelona GP generated over €300m in local economic activity in 2024, according to its own reports. This was reaffirmed by Barcelona circuit CEO Pol Gilbert as part of the track’s recent extension announcement, where he said that “Formula 1 generates an economic impact of more than €300 million per edition” at the venue.

F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali recently said the US GP at Austin generated “over $1 billion” for the local area in 2026, while the Las Vegas GP has generated over $3.2bn cumulatively for the local area over its three editions.

IFEMA Madrid chairman Jose Vicente de los Mozos said that the figures “confirm the strategic importance the Grand Prix has gained for Madrid’s economy and international profile from its very first edition, generating economic activity equivalent to 0.16% of the Madrid Region’s GDP and 0.30% of the city of Madrid’s GDP”.

The grand prix attracted 353,000 attendees. The survey estimates that 35% of visitors were from overseas and 20% travelling from elsewhere in Spain - meaning 45% were from Madrid and its immediate vicinity.

International visitors spent an average of €2,772 per person over the course of their stay - compared with €1,099 from Spanish visitors and €659 among Madrid residents - with those figures including the estimated average ticket price, which is not stated.

International visitors to the grand prix therefore spent 1.7 times that of an average international tourist to Madrid, and 2.9 times more than an international tourist visiting Spain. Domestic visitors spent 3.8 times more than a domestic tourist would on a trip to the Madrid region.

Local digital publication Democrata found that hotel prices averaged €485 - 70% more than usual - for the grand prix.

Around 49% of visitors stayed in hotels, 32% in short-term rental accommodation, and 19% with family and friends - generating €95m in tax revenues.

Short-term rentals have been a contentious issue for the local area in recent years as, in 2025, the Spanish government cracked down on Airbnbs, removing nearly 66,000 listings across the country and fining the company €64m for illegal listings.

Furthermore, residents local to the Madring protested its environmental and societal impact, including noise concerns.

The survey found that 95.3% of international attendees said the grand prix had ‘enhanced Madrid’s international image’ and 98.1% would recommend Madrid as a tourist destination, with 86% of attendees saying they were likely to return.

PwC partner Jordi Esteve said: “Through extensive fieldwork, we have found that grand prix visitors spend more and stay longer than the average visitor. This is helping Madrid attract high-value tourism, generating greater economic activity and supporting employment.”

PwC conducted 1,102 face-to-face surveys between the Friday and Sunday of the race weekend.

items.title: Ferrari's Leclerc-Hamilton problem is far from solved
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Don't be fooled by Ferrari's Formula 1 drivers playing nicely in Brazil; there are still very real tensions between Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

The drivers and team principal Fred Vasseur got together in Brazil to try to talk things through after Hamilton's extraordinary criticism of Leclerc following their victory-losing Mexico run-in.

That meeting proved constructive, and Leclerc and Hamilton were very well-behaved during the Brazilian Grand Prix, even following team orders and leaving each other plenty of room, unlike in Mexico.

Hamilton's summary was: "Everything's good. Fred brought us together. Fred was great in the meeting. And then he just left me and Charles to just give our points.

"We both had a really good, open discussion. And it's all good now. We'll just move on."

But you can't compare Mexico and Brazil, so Vasseur didn't bother reaching for what would have been an easy pat-on-the-back.

"You can't compare the two situations," Vasseur said, in respect of Leclerc and Hamilton's cordiality on-track at Interlagos.

"Honestly, we had a good discussion on Friday. We cleared the situation. We did a good reset on the mindset.

"They left my room joking together. It's good. I hope that it will last, to stay like this."

All Vasseur can do for now is "hope" it lasts because that Brazil fight was only ever going to be for minor points-paying positions, not a race win or a podium.

So there's every reason to believe that when the Ferrari is back fighting for wins, be it in Las Vegas or Qatar or Abu Dhabi, Hamilton and Leclerc are going to be back fighting tooth and nail.

After all, Leclerc admitted post-meeting: "Of course there is tension, of course we want to finish ahead of each other, and sometimes we are not going to do things right, and it's OK sometimes to disagree on the way you see things.

"But at the same time discussing about those helps a whole lot."

In light of the Leclerc-Hamilton tensions, Leclerc's ex-team-mate at Ferrari Carlos Sainz was asked about his time with Leclerc.

Hamilton had, after all, pointed to Leclerc's time alongside Sainz and Sebastian Vettel as evidence that he races his team-mates harder.

"I have relatively good memories of my time with Charles and the fights we had," Sainz said in Brazil.

"It is true that when you're fighting for wins, there's always more pressure, more things down the line. So you become naturally a bit more selfish than when you are fighting in the midfield for a P8 or a P9.

"It's more difficult maybe to follow exactly the ideal situation that the team would like you to follow, because there's a win down the line. There was wins down the line back then, but I always respected Charles. He always respected me. We never had contacts or anything like this. We just had strong fights. You remember Monza, Vegas. There was plenty of hot moments during the year.

"What was difficult more was the fanbase. The PR and the fanbase was really ignited back then, and it was very polarised between Charles and me. And I remember suffering a bit from the very hardcore fans of Charles insulting or wishing me bad.

"Maybe some Italian media also saying that I was not being enough of a number two when I needed to be, and vice-versa whenever Charles had to do it.

"So it's more the pressure surrounding Ferrari, that involves Ferrari, than the actual issues that I had with Charles, which were always resolved that same night when we called each other with a more cold head and we always managed to find the solution and the way forward."

Sainz felt it is an inevitable problem with having two equals in the same team.

"I cannot remember no Formula 1 team that has had two good drivers fighting at the front that haven't had issues when fighting for wins," Sainz added.

"You can choose whether to have a number two as a second driver, or you can have two good drivers that will create those issues. But you cannot have one without the other, in my opinion. And you will never have one without the other.

"Maybe in Ferrari it gets a bit exacerbated with everything that involves Ferrari, but I cannot remember a moment where this hasn't happened. It happened in Mercedes. It happened in McLaren the last few years. It happened in Ferrari.

"So I don’t know when it hasn't happened. It is part of Formula 1. And if you are a team principal and you know you're going to have two great drivers, you're always going to have that issue.

"I don't think you can ever calm those two guys 100% down and expect them not to go for a move for a race win."

Why Leclerc-Hamilton is different

There are some parallels to the tensions in 2019 when Leclerc managed to steal Ferrari away from four-time world champion Sebastian Vettel as a 21-year-old. This piece by Mark Hughes still stands as an excellent account of that.

Back then, the drivers were 'free to race', the team principal (Mattia Binotto) tried to play things fairly, the drivers were close enough in performance to routinely be near each other on track, and there was a huge battle for supremacy.

Leclerc ultimately won that battle convincingly, with Sainz brought into replace Vettel, but never as an equal to Leclerc. (That didn't mean he was a dutiful number two either. He was too quick for that.)

Leclerc and Sainz had their flashpoints, but ultimately things never uncontrollably spilt over for one good reason: Leclerc was ahead of Sainz around two-thirds of the time.

The dynamic therefore was very different: Leclerc even ended up helping Sainz to the only non-Verstappen victory of 2023 in Singapore. That was evidence of Leclerc playing the long game, knowing a small sacrifice there would only strengthen his position once Ferrari had a title-challenging car.

There was ultimately enough of a performance gap for there never to be too much needle between them. Leclerc didn't see Sainz as a threat to his position as Ferrari's spearhead. He was right, as Ferrari chose to replace Sainz with Hamilton just a few months after that Singapore win.

And it's no coincidence that in 2025, there being a clear performance gap between Leclerc and Hamilton meant there wasn't much needle between them.

Suddenly they're very closely matched in 2026, and the Leclerc-Vettel era tension is immediately re-exposed because now there is a threat to Leclerc's position. Leclerc was previously fairly comfortable, like Vettel was in 2015-18 as the focal point of the team, with team-mate Kimi Raikkonen very much a support act.

Now there is an active battle for supremacy. If Ferrari improves its power unit and has a title-challenging car next year, both Hamilton and Leclerc want to be the one leading that charge.

It's why the prospect of Ferrari's Brazil meeting being any kind of full stop on its Leclerc-Hamilton problem is absolute nonsense.

That's not going to change until Leclerc has destroyed another world champion - as he did to Vettel - or until he's the one destroyed by a team-mate.

items.title: MotoGP makes major US TV step with ESPN deal
items.author: Simon Patterson
items.content:
MotoGP has penned a new two-year deal for 2027 with broadcaster ESPN that will finally give the series a more permanent United States TV home, after a series of somewhat confusing contracts in recent seasons jumping around between different channels, platforms, and broadcasters.

The new deal, which will cover coverage not just in the US but also across Latin America, means ESPN becomes the exclusive rights holder for MotoGP, with a commitment to providing live or same-day coverage of every round.

Perhaps most importantly given the changing media landscape of recent years, it will also bring MotoGP onto one of the market’s major streaming platforms as it will appear on Disney+.

The news should come as welcome relief to US fans after quite a bit of uncertainty in recent years over where exactly to watch MotoGP.

Prior to 2020, the championship had a deal with BeIN Sports in which its team attended multiple races in person, before a move to NBC for four years.

But while that deal was notable for being with a major network, it meant MotoGP coverage jumping around between channels, with many races not airing live. A new deal for 2024 with TNT Sports (announced only hours before the start of the season) didn’t prove to be substantially different.

MotoGP moved to Fox in 2025, again announced only hours before the opening session of the first weekend, and again coverage moved around between channels, with this year’s American Grand Prix at Austin airing live on Fox Business.

With that in mind, the new ESPN deal should come as welcome news not just to MotoGP fans but to the series’ new Liberty Media owner, by providing a valuable growth platform as it attempts to replicate its success with Formula 1 in the US market.

"This agreement with ESPN marks an important milestone in MotoGP's growth strategy across the Americas,” said MotoGP’s deputy CEO Carlos Ezpleleta. 

“ESPN's position as one of the world's leading sports broadcasters, combined with its strong connection with audiences across the United States and Latin America, makes it the ideal platform for us to continue expanding MotoGP's reach and bring the sport closer to millions of people. 

“This is an exciting opportunity to introduce MotoGP to new audiences while continuing to serve our passionate existing fanbase through one of the most influential sports media brands in the world."

items.title: Hearing set for Audi Tsunoda appeal
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
The FIA has announced that Audi’s appeal against Yuki Tsunoda not getting a penalty at Formula 1’s Italian Grand Prix will be heard on November 25.

Audi complained after the Monza race for what it felt was an incorrect application of the rules against Tsunoda for an alleged grid infringement at the restart.

Tsunoda had been due to line up 14th but, after mistakenly initially heading towards the 15th-place grid slot, he veered at the last-minute to the right-hand side.

While he was able to come to a stop within his intended grid slot, so therefore was not out of position over the front, his Racing Bulls car had ended up at an angle.

That was enough for race director Rui Marques to decide to go for another formation lap because, according to a later stewards' document, "he stated he was not comfortable starting the race with the car in that position".

Tsunoda’s actions had triggered an FIA stewards’ investigation because drivers that cause an extra formation lap are deemed to be in breach of the rules.

Any driver who causes an additional formation lap but is able to start that lap is required to "enter the pitlane at the end of the lap and must start the [session] from the end of the pitlane".

With Tsunoda not serving that, F1's sporting regulations state that any unserved stop-and-go penalty is converted to a 30-second post-race time penalty.

Racing Bulls argued, however, that Tsunoda had not the extra formation lap - as he was still within his grid box and was not impacting any other drivers.

The stewards accepted that position and felt that Tsunoda himself had not been the “cause” of the extra formation lap – which was instead down to Marques’ own choice.

Audi complained, though, as it felt that Tsunoda had indeed been the catalyst for the extra formation lap.

It said in a short statement after Monza that it had "raised a concern regarding the application of Article B5.9.4".

Audi would stand to benefit were Tsunoda to be penalised, because a 30-second sanction would drop him to 15th - with Gabriel Bortoleto being promoted to 10th.

The matter will now be heard at the FIA’s International Court of Appeal in Paris on November 25. The hearing will take place behind closed doors at the request of the FIA, so no public nor media will be allowed to attend.

items.title: Tsolov gets twin F1 2027 reserve role to prepare him for race seat
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Red Bull has named Nikola Tsolov the official reserve driver of both of its Formula 1 teams in 2027 with a programme “designed to ensure he is fully prepared to race in F1 at the highest level”.

Tsolov missed out on a 2027 Racing Bulls seat as Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad were both handed extensions into next year. 

But Red Bull has made clear Tsolov is still very much the next driver in line for an F1 seat, confirming on the same day Lawson and Lindblad were confirmed for 2027 that Tsolov would be made reserve. 

Tsolov is currently fighting for the Formula 2 title with 2027 Haas F1 driver Rafael Camara and Alex Dunne, having taken six race wins with two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi remaining. 

Tsolov finished runner-up to Camara in his third Formula 3 campaign last year. 

Red Bull's announcement read: “In his new role, Nikola will undertake an extensive development programme, combining simulator and development work with valuable track experience through Free Practice sessions, Testing of Previous Cars (TPC), selected test sessions and tyre testing. 

“Alongside his responsibilities as a reserve driver, the programme is designed to ensure he is fully prepared to race in F1 at the highest level.” 

Tsolov said he was “incredibly happy and grateful” to Red Bull for the opportunity. 

“My ambition is clear: I want to become an F1 driver,” he said.

“Having the opportunity to spend next year preparing for that next step is incredibly exciting. I’m confident that with the team’s support and experience, I’ll have the best possible preparation to make sure I’m fully ready to take the next step onto the F1 grid when the time comes.” 

Tsolov impressed Racing Bulls with his FP1 debut in Mexico where he compared favourably to 2026 rookie Lindblad. 

“Nikola is an exceptionally talented young driver, and we have been hugely impressed by his development and performances over the past few years,” Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies said.

“To fight for the championship in F3 and now challenge for the F2 title in his first full season says a great deal about his ability and determination. 

“What has impressed us just as much is his maturity, his approach to racing and his willingness to keep learning and improving.

“We have enormous belief in Nikola’s potential and see him as a driver with a very exciting future in F1. 

“This appointment reflects our confidence in him and our commitment to his continued development. Our focus in 2027 will be on giving him the experience, tools and support he needs to be ready to race in F1 next.”

items.title: 'The most tradable sport nobody trades': Inside race prediction platform RPM
items.author: The Race Media
items.content:
RPM is the world’s first motorsport prediction platform, where every outcome of a race event becomes a tradable market. Fans are able to buy and sell outcomes on every moment of a race at a moment’s notice.

Founder Ben Jarrett joined The Race Business as part of our Spotlight series of interviews to explain how he spotted a niche in the motorsport market - and how RPM itself could play a part in changing how fans consume motorsport.

“RPM is at the intersection of motorsport, content creation, and prediction markets,” says Jarrett.

Will it rain? Who pits first? Which tyres do they choose?

Fans can essentially make predictions about every single facet of motorsport. And it’s an idea that was born out of a racetrack.

“I was racing GT4 cars, and I’m standing on the pitwall. Someone comes up and says: ‘10 bucks, he puts it into the wall at Turn 1’.

“The other guy’s like, ‘No, no, 100 bucks, he puts it [into the wall]’.

“Everyone was standing there. I was in my suit, I had my hands on my helmet, and we were supposed to go out there for practice before qualifying and put a lap in.”

It was at that moment that Jarrett had the idea to open up motorsport prediction markets to fans and content creators.

“I handed in my HANS device and my helmet to my mate and I drove home.”

He says the RPM app is as “simple as having a question that you want a large fanbase to help you solve. That’s a market: Max Verstappen to win in Australia, George Russell to make a pass for the lead on lap 10, or whenever”.

Jarrett says he’s found a gap in the market as motorsport fans don’t traditionally engage in iGaming - wagering on outcomes online - as other sports fans do, with football and basketball being the most popular sports in this regard.

“I would say there are 1.3 billion fans of motorsport. But in terms of iGaming volume, it provides less than half a percent.

“So, it's one of the most tradable sports on earth that nobody trades, that nobody touches.

“There are 72 days a year that F1 is on, and it’s becoming a part of people’s daily life.”

He points us to F1’s Global Fan Survey that, in 2025, found that 61% of motorsport fans engage with F1 content on a daily basis.

“So, this is a fan ecosystem that really is becoming part of people's daily life. And if we go and we look at social media… motorsport content is everywhere.”

RPM is also geared towards giving content creators their own space. Creators can build a standalone competition around an event - or keep the competition running all season with a running leaderboard - while RPM handles the predictions, scoring, credits, prizing support and league access.

Approved creators can even unlock revenue share opportunities with RPM in the future.

“I'm very interested in the content creators. And we use that word a lot because that's where we really see the opportunity. We want to give them a voice. We want to give them participation.

“We don't just see them as like a marketing push. We really see them as part of the heartbeat of what is RPM. This is a platform for them to come in, engage in motorsport on a daily basis, through markets, in a different way.”

items.title: Our verdict on Lawson earning a 2027 F1 extension
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will continue to race for Racing Bulls in 2027, with Red Bull electing against what would have been a huge Formula 1 driver sacking.

Here's what our team makes of the move to keep Lawson and Lindblad and not promote Formula 2 title contender Nikola Tsolov into a race seat.

An existential question has been answered

Very few driver decisions have felt as right as Lawson getting a fresh contract with Racing Bulls.

He has been superb this year. Yes, there are still some rough edges to smooth out, but he has been fast throughout, consistently strong, delivering technical input that his engineers have loved, and brilliantly able to shut out all the noise regarding the doubts over his future.

But there is a wider significance to Lawson getting a stay, and it's one I mentioned in Monday's From the Paddock newsletter. The Lawson decision was almost existential for Racing Bulls in telling us what that team is really about.

Sign up to our newsletter to be in with a chance of winning a signed Valtteri Bottas Cadillac F1 cap.

Is it an outfit that, under Alan Permane, can stand on its own two feet, take its own decisions and plot a path that is only focused on making itself better?

Or is it simply a puppet for sister squad Red Bull, a testing ground and training school for its future drivers, even if that means some short-term pain in rushing rookies through?

After the season Lawson has had, it would have made no sense for Racing Bulls to drop him and throw away all the good momentum it has built up. So keeping him for now gives us the answer about what Racing Bulls is about.

Tsolov has a bright future in F1, but time is on his side to make that step up.

The best decision for all involved

Pretty sure this is the best decision for Racing Bulls and in the future for Red Bull.

Both Lawson and Lindblad - a rookie, let's not forget - have shown that they can bring home the results when everything goes as planned over a race weekend.

Both are capable of being a replacement for Isack Hadjar or Max Verstappen if either of them slip on a banana skin. Red Bull knows what Lawson can bring to them if required, so he is a good measure of what Lindblad could potentially bring too.

Having Tsolov in the background and doing a few FP1 sessions will prepare him for an introduction in 2028.

As far as I'm concerned, it's the correct decision for all involved. 

Credibility for Racing Bulls

If Racing Bulls is to be at all seen as an F1 team in its own right, with its own ambitions and dreams and what have you, rather than a pure Red Bull talent farm, then yeah, Lawson pretty much had to be kept on.

Tsolov may end up faster down the line. For all we know, he may be faster already. But the kind of efficient scoring that Lawson has provided this year a rookie cannot match - I would say that's a rule in F1.

So Tsolov-for-Lawson would be nakedly sacrificing Racing Bulls's present for the senior Red Bull team's future, and every decision like that makes it less and less palatable for Red Bull to own two teams in F1.

Only if Racing Bulls has its own aspirations can it be allowed to continue, and a new deal for Lawson buys some credibility in my eyes.

Marko would have dropped Lawson long ago

At the height of his powers, Helmut Marko would have ditched Lawson ages ago.

Lawson had his shot at the top team, didn't make it, and will likely not be given that chance again.

Now Marko's no longer in charge, and this is the biggest indicator yet that Racing Bulls is not Toro Rosso; developing young drivers is no longer the only, or primary, end goal for this team.

You can't blame Red Bull. Instead of a team that cost and lost money to run like Toro Rosso, Racing Bulls is now a multi-billion dollar entity. Constructors' championship finishing position is not the only definition of value in an F1 business anymore.

Taking risks with a team built with the acceptance of losing money is one thing. Taking risks with a team worth billions is another.

None of this is to criticise the decision it has made, as Lawson is a worthy F1 driver. It's just to point out yet more evidence that Racing Bulls is acting and being run like its own team.

Lawson would be wise to find an exit route

Lawson is in a fantastic position now and has been one of the star drivers of the season, but he should already be thinking about exit routes for 2028.

Tsolov is going to be waiting in the wings next year, and there's no reason why Racing Bulls might be faced with the exact same 'three into two' dilemma for 2028.

This time Lawson was the overwhelmingly logical pick, next time he might not be and, given Red Bull leaves those decisions until late in the season, he doesn't want to suddenly be left without a seat for 2028.

So he'd be wise to try to follow the Pierre Gasly and Carlos Sainz playbook of finding another driver Red Bull decides it's done with you.

Adds to an excellent redemption arc

I've got a lot of time for this career redemption arc.

Lawson at the Red Bull senior team always felt like an uncomfortable fit to me, right from when it was announced. I certainly hadn't seen anything to suggest he would solve the team's second-driver problem.

Red Bull's bungling of what followed didn't help, but that ill-fated, two-race spell could've marked the beginning of the end of Lawson's F1 career.

Instead, what's followed has revealed plenty about his mental resolve - because he's had to process a lot these past 20 months yet has been absolutely unflappable. 

Driving for the top teams is what every driver craves, but it doesn't have to be the be-all and end-all and, if you don't make it, it doesn't automatically consign you to career collapse.

Lawson's proved emphatically this year that he deserves a place in F1. This contract extension was therefore the only acceptable outcome.

items.title: Red Bull's Lawson decision is a clean break from its Marko era
items.author: Edd Straw
items.content:
Lawson’s seat in Red Bull’s second team has been at very real risk in recent rounds, with Formula 2 race winner Nikola Tsolov waiting in the wings and Red Bull needing to decide which two of Lawson, Tsolov and Arvid Lindblad race for Racing Bulls next year. 

But had Lawson lost out - with zero options elsewhere on the grid to race in 2027 - it would have been an unprecedented move.

In the past 10 seasons of F1, there have only been two comparable cases of a driver doing as well as Lawson is currently doing, getting dropped and then not having an alternative seat for the following season.

Only Sergio Perez - who was eighth in the 2024 championship - and Alex Albon - who was seventh in the 2020 championship - have been higher placed than Lawson is right now (ninth) and yet found themselves without a drive the year after.

Both, of course, met that fate thanks to Red Bull, but the big difference is both Perez and Albon were driving for Red Bull Racing - and getting absolutely destroyed by Max Verstappen in the process.

Lawson is in a completely different situation here, in that he’s the highest-placed of all midfield drivers in the 2026 world championship and comfortably ahead of his rookie team-mate Lindblad.

The main threat to Lawson’s position comes from F2 title contender Tsolov. The Bulgarian has won six races in his rookie F2 season and sits only seven points behind 2027 Haas F1 driver and Ferrari junior Rafael Camara - who made his F1 debut in place of Esteban Ocon in Brazil.

Tsolov has made a strong case for promotion, not only because of those F2 results but also because of how well he did subbing for Lawson in a mandated rookie FP1 outing in Mexico, where Tsolov lapped within two tenths of Lindblad and generally looked very at ease with the whole business of being in F1.

On top of Tsolov’s impressive showing in Mexico, Lawson later had a run-in with Red Bull’s kingpin driver Verstappen during FP2 - which earned Lawson a strong rebuke from the four-time champion, in which Verstappen alluded to Lawson’s 2027 deal uncertainty.

The Race understands the recent triple-header has basically been the crunch moment for Red Bull and Racing Bulls to do their final analysis on who should drive next year - so Lawson been under pressure during this period and at genuine risk of losing his seat.

Which perhaps explains Verstappen’s pointed remark in the wake of their collision in Mexico, “It’s just not very smart behaviour when you’re in his position to pick a fight with me.”

But the way Lawson rebounded from that low point, recovering from a technical exclusion in qualifying and a pitlane start to finish seventh that weekend, in his familiar position as the leading midfield runner, showed true grit.

Add that to the way Lawson excelled in the wet in Brazil - fifth in qualifying and seventh in the race - and it’s difficult for anyone inside the Red Bull system to make the case he should definitely be dropped.

It has only been Lawson at real risk - because Lindblad has done an excellent job alongside him as a rookie and contributed a meaningful 35% of the points that leave Racing Bulls almost certain to finish fifth in the constructors’ championship - the highest place in the team’s history.

Lawson’s job within that team is essentially to give Red Bull a benchmark of performance to measure Lindblad against. There’s no realistic possibility of Lawson becoming a contender for a Red Bull Racing seat again, in the way there might still be for Lindblad or, eventually, Tsolov.

The trouble is that Lawson has done such an excellent job in his role this season - and has even taken a further step as a driver since subbing for Isack Hadjar at Red Bull for three races - that he made himself impossible to drop even though his presence no longer really fits the 'Red Bull conveyor belt' function Racing Bulls is supposed to have.

On Friday in Brazil, Racing Bulls team boss Alan Permane said Racing Bulls is trying to “apply a little bit of science” to the situation, a clear rebuke of the days when Helmut Marko would hire and fire junior drivers seemingly almost on a whim. 

“Red Bull's had a very successful young driver programme, and if I want to be... and I don't want to be critical of it, but I think if you guys are critical of it, maybe sometimes the drivers haven't been able to have enough time to settle, or maybe some snap decisions have been made,” Permane said.

Lawson’s average qualifying advantage over Lindblad is only seven hundredths of a second, but in the races - where the points are paid out - Lawson has a clear advantage.

He’s scored in 13 of the 17 grands prix he’s started for Racing Bulls this year, as well as taking points in three of the six sprint races staged. He’s also finished ahead of Lindblad 11 times out of the 14 races they have both finished and run ahead of him on 77% of the racing laps both completed.

That’s made him the undisputed king of the midfield. Of the 52 qualifying sessions and races, including sprints, held this year, Lawson has been classified at the top of that group 18 times.

To put that number in context, remember Alpine and Audi have made the fight at the front of that group a close one, and that Lawson wasn’t part of the midfield for eight of those because he was in Hadjar’s Red Bull.

His approach has also caught the eye. Prior to 2026, there were times when his decision-making in battle could be self-defeating. That led to more on-track incidents than necessary.

That’s something he’s largely cut out this year, while still fighting hard enough to get the results.

He’s also adapted well to the 2026 cars, recognising he needed to contain the desire to over-drive to get the most out of them - not easy to do for a driver who can be naturally aggressive on corner entries.

He’s also able to piece together weekends consistently well, often turning things round even if they start badly on Friday.He also did a good job in those three outings for Red Bull, despite the scars of what happened to him in 2025. That shows a mental robustness, which is also reflected in his mindset amid uncertainty about his future. He’s been able to focus on doing his job and not been distracted by this - something that is easier said than done.

Lawson explained: “A year ago I thought about it a lot. It was very much in my head and you just drive worse when you overthink things.”

Lawson hasn’t suddenly transformed himself into the best driver in F1. But he’s taken a big step to become a rounded, consistent, and dependable midfield performer - and a very quick one too.

That’s what eventually made him undroppable for 2027. 

Permane had already suggested “everyone will be happy” when the announcement finally came, so that suggests that now Lawson has been confirmed alternative arrangements will be made for Tsolov - which will most likely mean an official reserve driver role and an expanded programme of F1 testing and free practice running in 2027.

items.title: Racing Bulls officially keeps Lawson for 2027
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Liam Lawson will remain at Racing Bulls next season after the squad announced an unchanged Formula 1 line-up for 2027.

The New Zealander’s future had been uncertain for many weeks, with the Red Bull-owned outfit pondering whether to keep him on alongside Arvid Lindblad or promote its junior driver Nikola Tsolov.

However, as reported earlier this week, Lawson’s recent strong performances in Mexico and Brazil were understood to have put him on course for a new deal and convinced Racing Bulls he was the best candidate.

With Lawson currently sitting ninth in the drivers’ standings, as best of the rest behind the top four teams, and his contribution key to helping Racing Bulls sit fifth in the constructors’ championship, it would have been nonsensical to have dropped him.

Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane believed that the line-up of Lawson and Lindblad was the perfect one in terms of blending youth and experience.

“Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we’ve seen the progress they’ve made, both individually and as a pairing,” explained Permane.

“I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition. Together, we have a solid foundation to build on the progress made this year, continue pushing ourselves forward and take the next step towards achieving our ambitions in 2027."

Lawson has earned praise in the paddock this year for his standout performances for both Racing Bulls and during a stand-in run at Red Bull, when he filled in for the injured Isack Hadjar.

He thanked Racing Bulls for the belief in him.

“We've had a brilliant season together and the team has worked very hard to produce a fast car, which I've loved driving,” he said.

“It feels great to be part of a historic season for the team as we continue our fight for P5 in the constructors' championship.

"It's a testament to the hard work of everyone both at track, and back at the factory. I’m looking forward to carrying this momentum forward with Arvid through to 2027; we're building something super positive and I’m excited by what we can achieve together.”

The Racing Bulls statement that announced Lawson and Lindblad were staying for 2027 did not make any reference to plans for Tsolov, who is in the hunt to clinch the F2 crown this year.

The Bulgarian had a rookie FP1 run for Racing Bulls in Mexico, and will likely have a wider role with Red Bull in 2027. He has also been linked with a switch to Super Formula in Japan.

items.title: Russell launches fully-funded new karting academy
items.author: Fleur Mealing
items.content:
Mercedes Formula 1 driver George Russell has launched a new karting academy at Silverstone aimed at developing the next generation of motorsport talent, with 25 young drivers set to receive a fully funded championship opportunity in 2027.

The GR63 Karting Academy will be open to boys and girls aged eight and nine, with Russell hoping to provide a route into motorsport for talented youngsters who might otherwise be held back by the financial demands of the sport.

Based at Silverstone's karting circuit, the initiative will run across four stages, beginning with open-access qualifying sessions in December 2026.

The first stage will see eligible drivers compete in arrive-and-drive sessions between December 6 and 31, with the 80 fastest progressing to a shootout on January 31, 2027.

From there, 25 drivers will be selected for the GR63 Championship, an eight-round series running from March to November 2027. Each round will take place on a different circuit configuration at Silverstone, with all participation costs covered by the academy.

The 25 selected drivers will also receive a full set of academy equipment, including racing overalls, a helmet, gloves and boots.

The programme will culminate in December 2027, when the championship's top five finishers compete in a final race at Silverstone. Drivers will be evaluated on their talent, lap times, fitness, racecraft and media skills, with the overall winner receiving a fully-funded karting season in 2028.

Russell will help mentor and guide participants throughout the programme.

"Karting is where it all started for me, and it taught me everything I've relied on throughout my career," said Russell.

"I know how hard it is for talented young drivers to get that first opportunity, especially when budgets are tight.

"With the GR63 Karting Academy, I want to give something back by finding those hidden talents and giving them the support and platform they need to reach their potential."

The financial accessibility of the programme is a central part of its appeal. While the initial qualifying sessions will cost £25 and entry to the January shootout will cost £75, everything from the championship stage onwards will be fully funded.

The initiative is being supported by Silverstone and the British Racing Drivers' Club (BRDC), with BRDC president David Coulthard welcoming the opportunity to invest in Britain's motorsport future.

"The GR63 Academy captures that ethos perfectly, and we are delighted to work with George to support the next generation of drivers here at Silverstone," said Coulthard.

How to enter the GR63 Karting Academy

The initial arrive-and-drive qualifying sessions will take place at Silverstone Kart Track between December 6 and 31, 2026, at a cost of £25.

All applicants must be citizens of a Commonwealth country.

items.title: Why Mercedes cannot dominate F1's new era
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
They say history doesn't repeat itself, but it often rhymes. And that applies to Formula 1 as well.

The start of new-rules eras have often been hugely indicative of what is to come, as the trends of the inaugural season lay down the story of future years.

If we do some comparisons of the first years of the most recent major rules-change eras, we can see how the comparisons between the first and second half of each of those seasons gave us a hint of what was to come in the following campaigns.

Constructors' championship splits

Represented as first half / second half / total

: 112 / 60 / 172: 92.5 / 61.0 / 153.5: 14 / 57 / 71: 32 / 38 / 70: 34.5 / 25 / 59.5

: 366 / 335 / 701: 188 / 217 / 405: 121 / 199 / 320: 116 / 100 / 216: 96 / 85 / 181

2022 (22 rounds; 11 / 11)

: 359 / 400 / 759: 303 / 251 / 554: 237 / 278 / 515: 81 / 92 / 173: 81 / 78 / 159

2026 (23 rounds; 20 completed so far; 11 / 9)

: 379 / 273 / 652: 307 / 203 / 510: 177 / 238 / 415: 222 / 176 / 398

In 2009, Brawn GP took the crowns thanks to its stellar start to the year, but you could see Red Bull getting its act together ahead of what became its era of dominance.

In 2014, Mercedes was unstoppable and its advantage through the year clearly told us about it becoming the main force in F1.

In 2022, Ferrari started well but Red Bull got the weight off its car and pushed forward to begin Max Verstappen's real run of supremacy, off the back of his maiden title the year before.

For 2026, Mercedes has secured both crowns, but the story of the year is an intriguing one because a trend has emerged of there being no clear benchmark late on.

While Kimi Antonelli and George Russell kicked 2026 off strongly and laid title-winning foundations early on, subsequent spells of success for Red Bull, McLaren and Ferrari have pointed to a shift.

In fact, as the table below shows, if you take the results of the last five races up until and including Brazil, Mercedes is only the third-highest-scoring team.

Top four constructors (last five rounds)

Last five total points: 152Overall total: 415 (3rd0

Last five total points: 132Overall total: 510 (2nd)

Last five total points: 114Overall total: 652 (1st)

Last five total points: 92Overall total: 398 (4tth)

F1 has a super-close top four where no team seems to have been able to edge clear of its rivals, and it has been hard to pick out anyone who has built up some momentum.

This is why, for all the joy that Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has taken from getting his team back to title-winning ways, he has no sense that this is the start of "runaway" success.

"It looks like the most competitive era that is about to start," he said.

"The teams have become so professional in capability and resource that these kind of runaway seasons, I don't see them anymore, whether it's four in a row or eight in a row. And that is a completely new challenge.

"You can see how quickly it goes from you being dominant and within a few races you realise that your upgrade doesn't work and you fall back and you're just third on the road. So it's great for the sport.

"I wish it was the era of Mercedes and me running away with another few championships. I don't think it's the reality."

The upgrade war seems to have had the effect of repeatedly shuffling the order of the top four.

Whenever any of the major teams have brought big development steps, often those have helped push them to the front and changed the hierarchy.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has labelled this "ping pong season" in terms of how teams bounce between being at the front or the back of that top-four block.

"Anybody that upgrades kind of takes an advantage, but even if you do a good job of developing, not necessarily [is it the case that] you can establish yourself at the top," he said recently.

"We have a variable level of supremacy, dependent on the track conditions or the optimisation of the set-up.

"But the reality is that I think nowhere before we have had F1 so competitive and with such a rate of development. If we raced with the race-one car [from the Australia season opener], we will be one and a half seconds slower than what we are at the moment."

The cause of this major shuffling is not only the fact that the big teams all seem to be so evenly matched in terms of their capability. (And have found ways to all keep pushing on with developments under the cost cap.)

It is that the FIA appears to have made life very difficult for teams because the aero regulations are so restrictive, leaving designers with only very small areas they can work on.

Focused on creating cars that did not produce significant dirty air, the FIA was determined not to allow areas that teams could exploit to ruin this and improve downforce.

And this has left teams capped in terms of how much performance they have been able to eke out.

Stella added: "If you take the regulations and you define the volumes within which you can put aerodynamic devices, that's not how an aerodynamicist would do it.

"They [the rules] have been done in a certain way somehow to jeopardise for the sake of competition and also for the sake of allowing the following and the overtaking."

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies agreed on the lack of design freedom leading to diminishing returns for all teams.

"The convergence is probably happening earlier than what we all thought," he said. "I'm guessing somehow, it's perhaps an indication of fairly restrictive regulations.

"That being said, you see cars with visibly different concepts and you see four top teams fighting, which is probably a great point to be for the sport.

"So, let's see how it will pan out in the second year. But to be already in the second part of '26 in situations where you turn up at the race weekend and you don't know which one of the four top teams is going to win the race, I think it's great for the sport."

The end result of all this is a form book that is in a state of flux.

Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur thought that the 'ping pong' element of rapidly shuffling fortunes was a consequence of immature rules offering potential for big gains, something that will slow down into next season where he felt teams would converge more.

"Each time that we were bringing something, we are doing a step," he said. "That was a little bit the story of the season because, as we [the top-four teams] were not bringing upgrades at the same races, you have this kind of rotation.

"Probably it could be less through next year and the following years, but we will have a kind of convergence of performance of where we are next year."

And it's for this reason that Wolff was convinced that it is important Mercedes gets back to its early performance levels now that give it a springboard into next year.

"Look at the last few races: we haven't won [Mercedes has one win in the last five]," he said in Brazil.

"The competition has been getting tougher, between Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull and ourselves. It's four teams that can win races and will be challenging for a world championship. And I have no doubt that it's going to be very difficult for us next year.

"For me, the 2027 season has started now."

items.title: Hamilton loses 'most marketable athlete' status in 2026
items.author: Samarth Kanal
items.content:
Lewis Hamilton is no longer sport’s most marketable athlete - or even the most marketable Formula 1 driver, having fallen behind Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc - in the latest rankings created by media and events business SportsPro.

Hamilton was top of the 2025 SportsPro marketability rankings for athletes, with a total marketability score of 96.03 out of 100.

In 2026, Hamilton is ranked 22nd. His marketability score is 66.63, on par with footballers Neymar and Vinicius Junior.

Hamilton’s team-mate Leclerc is ahead in ninth on the list with a marketability score of 71.12, up from 25th in the 2025 list with a score of 75.03. 

The next-highest driver is Max Verstappen (48th, up from 81st last year), while 2025 champion Lando Norris (78th) is now ranked behind McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri (56th) having been 23 places ahead in 41st last year.

New champion Kimi Antonelli is the lowest placed F1 driver who made the top 150 in 126th, a 48-place drop from 78th in 2025.

MotoGP rider Marc Marquez is the only motorsport athlete not tied to F1 on the list, ranking 86th, five places above Alpine F1 driver Pierre Gasly.

Belarusian tennis player Aryna Sabalenka is top of the list with, ahead of Chinese skier Eileen Gu, Greek basketball player Giannis Antetokounmpo, Norwegian footballer Erling Haaland, and Spanish tennis player Carlos Alcaraz.

American athletes make up 32% of the top 150 while British and Indian athletes are next with 7.3% of the pie apiece.

Football (soccer) has 33 athletes on the list and a 22% share of the list while motorsport’s eight representatives (5.3%) put it sixth on the list of sports, behind tennis and cricket but ahead of golf and boxing. 

Female NASCAR driver Toni Breidinger and F1 driver Liam Lawson dropped off the list having appeared in 2025.

How the marketability scores are calculated - why is Hamilton lower than Leclerc?

The marketability score is a combination of brand equity, momentum, and commercial trajectory, three metrics that are calculated by combining "several hundred data points" and more than 3000 brand partnership records over July 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026.

Scroll down to see how the motorsport athletes rank within the top 150.

Brand equity is the strength and trust of the athlete’s brand, momentum is the rate at which the athlete’s value is growing, and commercial trajectory is the room for an athlete’s future commercial growth. 

The latter metric is given the smallest weighting out of the three, and the scores are relative rather than absolute; Sabalenka’s ranking puts her top with the other athletes in mind. 

Leclerc, 29, has a higher brand equity score than Hamilton but a lower momentum score. The Monegasque’s ranking of commercial trajectory also boosts his ranking compared to Hamilton.

Age and longevity in the sport has an impact on the trajectory score: at 41 Hamilton is the joint-oldest athlete on the list with Cristiano Ronaldo and LeBron James.

Furthermore, Leclerc scores highly on the commercial trajectory metric, implying that there is strength in his brand that hasn’t been converted into commercial returns compared to Hamilton.

Leclerc scores high in brand equity due to his personal style and public presentation, plus the size of his audience and how actively that audience engages with his brand. 

Chris Collins, president of NorthStar (which powers the rankings) said to BlackBook Motorsport that Leclerc has "one of the strongest established brands of any athlete in the world.

"He ranks second of all 247 athletes we assessed on brand equity, built on how he presents himself, a compelling personal story and premium partners who keep choosing to work with him.

"As one of the most-followed drivers on the grid, it’s little surprise to see his audience scores performing well, but it also emphasises that his followers actively interact with his profile. He also benefits from a high audience breadth score, an expected outcome for all Formula 1 drivers thanks to their global profile."

He added of Hamilton: "What keeps him below the top 10 isn’t his brand, it’s time. At 41, there is naturally less career runway ahead, and a forward-looking assessment should read a great career in its later chapters exactly that way."

items.title: What we know about worrying new Honda F1 reliability issue
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Honda's worrying return of reliability problems includes a new issue, the root cause of which it might not trace before the end of the Formula 1 season.

Aston Martin and engine partner Honda suffered their third DNF of the triple-header in Brazil, when Lance Stroll retired for the second race in a row.

Stroll had two separate battery problems over the course of the Brazil weekend and didn't make it to mid-distance in Sunday's grand prix.

It means Stroll has finished just six of the 20 races held this season, while team-mate Fernando Alonso has had seven retirements of his own.

There have been some flashes of optimism - in relative terms, given how disastrous this first season of the new alliance has been - of late as Alonso scored points in Malaysia five races ago, had surprisingly good pace at Austin despite sustaining significant floor damage on the opening lap, and excelled in the wet in Brazil.

There, Alonso comfortably gave Aston Martin and Honda their best qualifying of the year, getting into Q3 for the first time and lining up eighth on the grid.

But this has been badly undercut by a return of significant fragility that's closer to how badly Honda started 2026.

Reliability problems also put paid to Alonso's chances in Mexico, where he had looked quite competitive and closer to the top 10 than normal. The issue was related to the cooling system inside the energy recovery system, whereas in Brazil the emergence of battery problems for Stroll sounded a clear alarm bell.

Shintaro Orihara, Honda's lead trackside engineer, acknowledged that "we know what happened, but we don't know what is the root cause".

He admitted it may take a few weeks to find that, but already from the data there needs to be some kind of countermeasure for the next race in Las Vegas, while Honda traces the underlying cause so it can be addressed properly for 2027.

"We need to find the actual root cause of this error for next year," he said.

"Otherwise, we keep having the same issue."

This was a different kind of failure to what had occurred in Mexico, which had led to MGU-K problems. But the theme is similar: in Mexico, Orihara had admitted to a lack of robustness within Honda's engine in more ways than one, and the fault there hadn't shown up in simulation.

Now Honda knows what happened but doesn't know why. That's a worrying through-line between the two issues. It also harks back to the start of the year, when Honda could identify the obvious catastrophic consequences of the problems that were emerging and could see broadly where they came from, but didn't know exactly what the problem's root was, because it had come out of the blue compared with what it had experienced on the dyno.

What's particularly alarming is that this does seem to be a regression from where Honda had got to in the middle of the season.

Its performance was obviously still lacking, and its engine is still underpowered on the internal combustion side, even with upgrades through the year to try to trim the deficit.

But it had at least got to a point where its cars were finishing races, which allowed Alonso to score some points when the Aston Martin was heavily upgraded.

Either side of the summer break, Alonso had five straight finishes, and Stroll got two of his six finishes this year in three races before the summer break too.

Orihara acknowledged that reliability was simply better in the middle of the season, but that has been replaced by "several issues" in recent races.

Some of this trend could be related to the mileage of parts - components simply coming to the end of their life cycle - or to just a case of Honda trying to run the engine harder for performance and going over the edge.

But with the battery issue that emerged in Brazil specifically, it's too early to say what the trigger was.

Honda has not made the progress it would have hoped for this season in terms of the all-round performance of the engine, and at best has only achieved some of its performance targets in very specific circumstances.

So the fact that reliability has got worse, without a clear upside, puts Honda under pressure and brings an unfortunate amount of negative scrutiny again, right at the end of a year in which it has had to come through quite a lot of adversity.

It is also a curveball for the development work Honda is doing on 2027, when it needs to take a step in both performance and reliability.

Everything that has been indicated so far is that there will not be a major step at the start of the new season. There's already a plan to phase in further upgrades through the year. But that work will already be deeply under way.

Troubleshooting takes away human resource, limited dyno hours which are restricted under F1's engine development limits, money that comes under the engine cost cap, and simply time because the clock is ticking to the start of 2027.

First the cooling issue in Mexico, whatever that was exactly, and now this on the battery side, takes Honda's focus away from a path that it would ideally be a lot further down.

Honda CEO Toshihiro Mibe was in Brazil, which Orihara said has a galvanising effect on the staff - "but on the other hand, we had a battery issue twice this weekend".

It was not exactly how Honda's F1 operation would have liked to present itself in front of the big boss. But, as Orihara noted, Mibe at least "knows what is happening trackside".

"He will bring this experience to the Japanese side and also boost our development," said Orihara.

If there was ever any possibility of complacency creeping in about how much work Honda has to do to reach the necessary standard, the CEO seeing first-hand the kind of problems still being encountered this deep into 2026 will have stamped it out.

items.title: F1's divisive wet weather tyres to change in 2027 - what needs solving
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Formula 1 tyre supplier Pirelli is close to finalising new specification wet-weather tyres for next season that already address concerns drivers voiced last weekend.

F1 had its first proper wet weekend of the year at Interlagos, with both qualifying and the race impacted by the rain.

Saturday’s running took place in conditions that were so extreme that the wet tyre, which has rarely been used in recent years, became the preferred choice for the conditions.

The race on Sunday was hit by showers, with drivers starting on intermediates, shifting to slicks and then reverting to inters towards the end when the rain returned.

But despite there being no major incidents – and the race being the first this year not interrupted by either a virtual or full safety car – drivers were still unhappy with how the wet rubber behaved.

Williams driver Carlos Sainz called for work to be done with Pirelli to deliver improvements in the future.

“The level of the wet and the inter is not good enough and we need to work with Pirelli on finding a better tyre,” he said. 

“In the mixed conditions, the inter is still a very weak tyre at the rear, by the time it warms up the front is gone.

“And the extreme [wet], honestly, we had so much aquaplaning and a big lack of rear grip. So still missing a bit of development on these two tyres.” 

The biggest challenge that drivers faced with the intermediate tyre on Sunday was getting them up to operating temperature.

This proved especially challenging on the low-speed laps to the grid, where a number of drivers were seen battling to keep their cars on the track.

And things weren't much better in the race, as Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson said it had been a real challenge to get the tyres into the right operating window.

The biggest problem was the temperature was much cooler,” Lawson said. “So even though there was less water on the laps of the grid, the cars were nearly undriveable. And the temps were just going down.

“We survived the start of the race, but at points when it rains a lot, it's not that the standing water is too much; it's that you can't actually keep the temperature in it. So, if we're on a track like Vegas and it rains, honestly, I think we're in trouble.”

But it was not just the fire-up that was a problem, as the inters proved very delicate in the race too.

Alex Albon, who described the laps to the grid as “insane”, said things were not much better once the tyres were up to temperature.

“It just feels like they never overheat or they never get up to temperature," he explained. "Then by the time you're circulating, the tread's already come off the tyre and then you're already struggling, you're sliding around.

“So you never feel good at any point in the race; it never feels like it comes alive.”

One of the common themes across this season is that the intermediate tyres feel worse than the previous version.

Alpine’s Pierre Gasly, who has long been sceptical about the inters ever since he tried them out at a wet test earlier this year, feels like they don't give as much confidence to push on as their predecessor.

“Generally, I must say they feel very poor,” he said. “The grip, I don't know if it's only with our car, but compared to the inters we used to have in the previous years, it just feels like they're nowhere. Extremely poor grip.

“The last stint felt [in Brazil] like I was driving on ice.  So I want to review exactly what happened with our car. I don't know if it was the case for everyone, but it's genuinely not a very good tyre.”

Gasly's point is well-founded because Pirelli has had to design a tyre for the 2026 rules that is theoretically a step away from what is ideal.

The switch between straight mode and corner mode at the end of straights puts huge forces through the tyres, plus Pirelli needs to ensure its product can cope if active aero fails and cars are running down straights with maximum downforce.

So in a similar vein to how straight mode consequences have forced increases in minimum slick tyre pressures, Pirelli had to make a more robust intermediate tyre.

Furthermore, the minimum pressures have also gone up for wets and inters. In Brazil, for example, the minimum front pressures went up from 25.5psi last year on the inters to 28psi now, and on the wets from 22psi to 26.5psi.

The impact is a tyre that does not move around as much - which does not inspire confidence from the drivers to lean on and is also much harder to warm up.

The circumstances of the rule changes are something that Haas driver Ollie Bearman referenced in Brazil.

“They are definitely a bit worse than last year’s ones,” he said. “There’s a few more parameters that the manufacturer has to put in mind when they design these tyres, because of the straight mode, ride heights and things like that.

“The tyre feels a bit less forgiving: very stiff, very hard to warm up. Lap 1 was a big challenge. It’s a warm-up thing again for us, same as yesterday in quali.”

And while drivers did manage to get through the Brazilian weekend, Interlagos has a rough track surface and a twisty infield section that helps put temperature into the rubber. That may not be true at all venues on the calendar.

As Mercedes driver George Russell said: “I think it's important also to realise the three tracks driven on were very rough tarmacs and Malaysia was hot even in the rain.

“Singapore sprint race was still hot and [Brazil qualifying], even though it was raining, it was 30 degrees and the track was 30 degrees. Maybe in 15 degrees of Spa, we're giving different feedback.”

What Pirelli is looking to change

Pirelli always knew that it would need to fine-tune its wet tyres to the real 2026 cars, with the current designs having been based on feedback from mule car running last year.

It had planned a wet test in Bahrain in February to help it work on understanding things better using an artificially soaked track, but that had to be abandoned in the wake of the Iran war beginning.

Further wet weather tests over the season have been completed, which has put Pirelli on a path to introduce revised inters and wets for next season.

While Pirelli motorsport boss Dario Marrafuschi does not want to reveal too many specifics about what is coming for 2027, he has confirmed that the warm-up issues on the inter will be addressed.

“Tyre development is going ahead and we have a different spec for next year,” he told The Race.

"Some of the drivers were complaining about warm-up, so we have been working for next year on the warm-up phase, on the intermediates.”

He added: “It doesn't mean we are not satisfied with this year's specs because we had very good racing in Malaysia, in Singapore and in Brazil as well. But an optimisation can be done.

“We always listen quite openly to the comments of the drivers."

The final homologation of the wet and inter tyre designs with the FIA will be made in December, when more details will be revealed about what is changing for next year.

But Marrafuschi also believes there is an element that, in the meantime, teams will get a better handle on how to get more from the inter now that they have some proper experience of it.

He thinks what was highlighted in Brazil was how some squads and drivers seem to have had a better understanding of what was needed than others.

“Clearly there are some cars or drivers, some set-ups or whatever, that are more comfortable in one condition or the other," he explained.

“We saw in the beginning of the race, Lewis [Hamilton] having an astonishing performance, with zero warm-up problems at all. 

"We know that other drivers, since the formation laps, were complaining about the front-end warm-up. So, there are some tunings that are in the hands of the teams.”

items.title: Liberty Media founder sells voting power of F1's parent company
items.author: Samarth Kanal
items.content:
Liberty Media founder and ex-chairman John Malone has sold his significant voting power in Formula 1's parent company.

Malone founded Liberty Media in 1991 and stepped down as chairman of the board in 2026, nine years after Liberty Media acquired F1 for $4.6billion USD (£3.4bn).

Malone was the most significant voting shareholder of Liberty Media until early November 2026 when Liberty Media announced that it had purchased Malone's 'high-vote' stock and exchanged it for 'low-vote' stock, essentially diluting Malone's voting power from around 48% to 3%.

Liberty Media purchased the high-vote stock after Malone received "a number of unsolicited offers from third parties" to acquire it.

The transaction effectively eliminates the transfer of Malone's voting power to a third party and strengthens Liberty Media shareholders' power in voting matters - such as a sale of F1.

In 2025, Malone said on the Opening Bid Unfiltered finance podcast that Liberty would be open to a sale of F1 - with the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund (PIF) among F1's then-touted suitors.

He said F1 "has an exceptionally good economic structure", adding: "It's a public company. If somebody gets carried away, and they want to buy it, and they're willing to pay more for it than the board thinks that they can deliver to the shareholders, then we would sell it. That's the bottom line."

Liberty Media president and CEO Derek Chang said during the company's Q3 earnings call that Malone "controlled a significant set of votes with a relatively low economic interest".

He explained that Liberty Media's purchase of the voting shares "helps us effectively control our own destiny forward".

There is no indication that Liberty Media is considering a sale of F1 in 2026.

Chang added: "We're still focused primarily on growing the businesses that we have. And as we stated previously, sort of investing behind those businesses and growth plans that they have is probably the biggest priority as we think about other forms of capital allocation."

The net worth of F1 sits at nearly $28bn as of November 2026, with the average value of an F1 team having reached $3.6bn in 2025 according to Forbes.

In 2025, Liberty Media completed its acquisition of an 84% stake in MotoGP commercial rights holder Dorna for around $3.3bn or €3.02bn.
